title: Giant Mirrors and a Universe of Galaxies
summary: A man named George Ellery Hale kept building bigger and bigger mirror telescopes on California mountaintops. With one of them, Edwin Hubble found a special blinking star in a fuzzy cloud called Andromeda and proved it was a whole other galaxy. Suddenly the universe was full of galaxies, and they were all rushing apart!

sections.heading: The Boy Who Built Observatories
paragraphs: Some people collect stamps. George Ellery Hale collected telescopes, and then, when he grew up, he collected the money to build the biggest ones on Earth. Four times in his life he helped create the largest telescope of its kind in the world, a record few people, if anyone, have ever matched.

Hale was born in Chicago on 29 June 1868. His father had grown rich making elevators for the city's new tall buildings, and he was happy to spend money on his curious son. By the time George was 14 he had his first telescope, and soon he had a real laboratory in the family home, packed with prisms, batteries and chemicals. As a teenager he set up his own little observatory behind the house, called the Kenwood Observatory.

Hale did not mainly want to look at pretty sights. He wanted to understand what stars actually are, and the nearest star is the Sun. While he was still a student at MIT, around 1890, he invented a clever instrument called the spectroheliograph. It photographed the Sun in the light of just one color, the color given off by one single chemical element. That way you could see where, say, glowing calcium or hydrogen gas was swirling on the Sun's surface.

Hale was also a born organizer. He became editor of the Astrophysical Journal, which became the most important astronomy magazine in the world, and in the 1890s he persuaded the Chicago businessman Charles Yerkes to pay for the giant Yerkes refractor that you met in Part 11. But as soon as that great lens was working, Hale realized something that would shape the rest of his life: lenses had reached their limit. A lens can only be held at its edges, so a very big one sags under its own weight. A mirror, on the other hand, can be supported from behind across its whole back. The future, he decided, belonged to mirrors.

He also realized that a great telescope in a smoky, cloudy city was wasted. Light from street lamps and the wobbling air near the ground blurred everything. In 1903 he made the hard trip up a rough trail to the top of Mount Wilson, a peak about 1,740 meters (5,700 feet) high above Pasadena in Southern California. The air there was often wonderfully calm and steady, and the sky was dark. Hale fell in love with the place.

Now he needed money, a lot of it. Luckily, the steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie had just set up the Carnegie Institution of Washington to fund science. In 1904 Hale won its support, and the Mount Wilson Solar Observatory was born. At first it was mainly for studying the Sun, and in 1908 Hale made one of the great discoveries of solar science there: sunspots are giant regions of powerful magnetism. He showed this by looking at how the spectral lines in sunlight from a sunspot split apart, a sign of strong magnetic fields.

sections.heading: Mules, a Mountain and the 60-Inch
paragraphs: Hale already had a mirror waiting. Back in 1896 his father had bought him a 60-inch (1.5-meter) glass disk, cast by the famous Saint-Gobain glassworks in France. The disk weighed about 860 kilograms (1,900 pounds), about as much as a small car. It had been sitting around for years because there was no telescope to put it in.

Turning a plain glass disk into a telescope mirror is slow, careful work. The front must be ground into a curve called a paraboloid, a shape like a very shallow bowl that sends all the starlight that hits it to one single point. Grinding started in 1905 and took about two years. The optician George Willis Ritchey worked the glass with rotating tools and grinding powder, testing it again and again until the surface was correct to a tiny fraction of the width of a hair. Then a thin coating of silver was laid on the glass to make it shine like a mirror.

Getting all the heavy parts to the top of Mount Wilson was an adventure of its own. There was no paved road up the mountain in those days, only a narrow, twisting trail. Steel parts, building materials and equipment were hauled up by mule trains and, later, by special trucks crawling along a widened path. One of the young men who drove the mules up and down the mountain was a teenager named Milton Humason. Remember his name, because he will come back in this story as a scientist.

The 60-inch telescope saw first light on 13 December 1908. First light is what astronomers call the very first time starlight enters a new telescope. The 60-inch was immediately the largest working telescope in the world. It was used to take photographs of nebulae and to spread the light of stars into spectra, and it showed what a big mirror on a good mountain could do.
But Hale was already dreaming bigger. Even before the 60-inch was finished, he had found a new donor.

sections.heading: The Hooker 100-Inch: King of the Mountain
paragraphs: John D. Hooker was a Los Angeles businessman who loved science. In 1906 he gave Hale 45,000 dollars to buy and grind a mirror 100 inches (2.5 meters) across. It would collect almost three times as much light as the 60-inch, because the light a mirror catches depends on its area, not just its width.

Saint-Gobain in France was asked to cast the glass. Making a disk that large was at the edge of what any factory could do. The French glassmakers cast it in 1906 from several batches of molten glass, and when the finished disk arrived in California in 1908 people were alarmed: it was full of small bubbles and layers. Some feared it could never hold a perfect curve. After much worry and many tests, Ritchey and his team decided to try anyway. Grinding and polishing took years, and in the end the mirror turned out superbly well.

The telescope that would hold it was a monster for its time. The whole moving structure weighed about 100 tons, yet it had to turn smoothly enough to follow a star across the sky for hours. To make that easier, much of its weight floated on a bath of mercury, a heavy liquid metal, so that it could be turned with surprisingly little effort. A huge dome was built around it on the mountaintop.

The Hooker telescope saw first light on 2 November 1917. According to a story often told at Mount Wilson, the first images that night looked terrible, smeared into several overlapping blobs, and Hale went to bed fearing disaster. When the team looked again after midnight, the stars were sharp. The dome had been left open during the day, and the Sun had warmed the mirror unevenly; as the glass cooled in the night air, it settled into its correct shape. Whether or not every detail of that story is exact, it teaches a real lesson that telescope builders still worry about: a big mirror must be at the same temperature as the air around it.

For the next 30 years, the Hooker would be the largest telescope on Earth, and it was used for some of the most important observations in the history of science. In 1920 the physicist Albert Michelson fitted it with a special attachment, a stellar interferometer, which used two small mirrors set far apart on a beam across the top of the telescope. With it, astronomers measured the size of the giant red star Betelgeuse in Orion. It was the first time anyone had measured the width of a star other than the Sun.

Meanwhile, the mule driver Milton Humason had come back to Mount Wilson in 1917 as a janitor. He had left school at 14 and had no diploma at all. But he loved the telescopes, and he started volunteering as a night assistant, helping astronomers with their equipment. He turned out to be astonishingly skillful and patient at the telescope. In 1919 Hale made him a member of the scientific staff, a very unusual step for someone without even a high school diploma. That same year, a tall, confident young astronomer named Edwin Hubble arrived on the mountain.

sections.heading: The Great Debate: How Big Is Everything?
paragraphs: By 1920, astronomers had photographed thousands of faint, fuzzy patches in the sky called nebulae, from the Latin word for clouds. Many of them had a beautiful spiral shape, like a pinwheel or a whirlpool, just as Lord Rosse had sketched in 1845. The biggest and brightest was in the constellation Andromeda. On a dark night you can see it with no telescope at all as a faint smudge. The Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described it as a little cloud in his Book of Fixed Stars around the year 964.

The huge question was: what are these spirals? One idea said they were fairly small, nearby clouds of gas, maybe new solar systems forming, all inside our own Milky Way. In that case the Milky Way was the whole universe. The other idea, sometimes called the island universe theory, said each spiral was a gigantic, faraway collection of billions of stars, a whole galaxy as big as our own, so distant that it looked like a tiny smudge.

On 26 April 1920, two astronomers argued the question in front of the National Academy of Sciences, at the Smithsonian's U.S. National Museum in Washington, D.C. Each gave a talk of about 40 minutes. It is remembered today as the Great Debate.

On one side stood Harlow Shapley, a brilliant young astronomer from Mount Wilson. Using the 60-inch telescope and Henrietta Leavitt's Cepheid ruler, he had measured the distances to big ball-shaped star clusters and found that the Milky Way was enormous, perhaps 300,000 light-years across, far bigger than anyone had thought. He also showed that the Sun is not at the center of the Milky Way but far out toward its edge. If the Milky Way was that huge, he argued, the spirals were probably just parts of it.

Shapley had some evidence that sounded strong. Another Mount Wilson astronomer, Adriaan van Maanen, claimed to have measured the spiral nebulae slowly turning on photographs taken years apart. If the spirals were really far away, then to turn that much they would have to spin faster than light, which is impossible. Shapley also pointed to a 'new star' that had blazed up in Andromeda in 1885 and briefly shone almost as brightly as the whole nebula. How could a single star outshine a whole galaxy?

On the other side stood Heber Curtis of the Lick Observatory. He thought the Milky Way was smaller, about 30,000 light-years across, and that the spirals were separate island universes. He pointed out that astronomers had spotted more exploding stars, called novae, in the Andromeda nebula than in any area of similar size in the Milky Way, and that those novae looked very faint, which suggested they were very far away. He noted that spirals were moving away from us at huge speeds, measured by Vesto Slipher, too fast to be held by the Milky Way's gravity. And he explained why no spirals were seen along the band of the Milky Way: thick dark dust in our galaxy's flat disk blocks the view.

So who won? In a way, both did. Shapley was closer to correct about the size of the Milky Way and right that the Sun is far from its center. Curtis was right about the biggest question: the spirals are galaxies of their own. Van Maanen's measurements of spinning nebulae turned out to be mistakes, and the bright 1885 'nova' in Andromeda was really a supernova, a far more powerful explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. But in 1920 nobody could prove any of this. They needed a measurement, not an argument.

sections.heading: VAR! The Star That Changed the Universe
paragraphs: Edwin Hubble was born in 1889 in Marshfield, Missouri. As a young man he was a star athlete. He studied science at the University of Chicago, then went to Oxford University in England as a Rhodes Scholar, where he studied law, partly to please his father. He even served as an officer in the U.S. Army in World War I. But astronomy kept pulling him back. He earned his PhD at Yerkes Observatory and in 1919 joined the staff at Mount Wilson, where he could use the most powerful telescope on Earth.

Hubble set out to photograph the Andromeda nebula again and again, hunting for novae. On the night of 5 October 1923, continuing into the early hours of 6 October, he took a 45-minute exposure with the Hooker telescope. The air was unsteady that night, but the plate showed something interesting. A photographic plate is a sheet of glass coated with light-sensitive chemicals, the ancestor of a digital camera sensor. Hubble spotted three tiny dots that he thought might be novae, and marked each one with the letter N.

Then he did the careful part. He compared his new plate with older plates of the same patch of Andromeda, taken over many years by other astronomers. One of his 'novae' was not a nova at all. It was there on some old plates, faint on others, brighter on some. It was getting brighter and fainter over and over again, like a slow heartbeat. Hubble crossed out the N and, in excited capital letters, wrote 'VAR!' beside it, short for variable star. That glass plate still exists at the Carnegie Observatories, and it is one of the most famous objects in the history of astronomy.

By studying the star over many nights, Hubble found that it brightened and dimmed with a period of about 31.4 days. That pattern meant it was a Cepheid variable, exactly the kind of star Henrietta Leavitt had studied at Harvard (Part 12). Leavitt had discovered that a Cepheid's period tells you its true brightness: the slower it pulses, the more powerful it really is. Once you know how bright a star truly is, and you measure how bright it appears, you can work out its distance, just as you can judge how far away a streetlight is if you know its real wattage.

Hubble did the math. The answer was astonishing. The star, now called V1, was roughly a million light-years away. By the end of 1924, after finding a dozen Cepheids, he settled on about 900,000 light-years. Even Shapley's giant Milky Way was only about 300,000 light-years across. The Andromeda nebula had to lie far outside our galaxy. It was a galaxy itself.

Hubble was a careful, even cautious, man, and he waited until he had more stars before going public. His results were read aloud at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Washington, D.C., on New Year's Day 1925. According to the astronomer Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin, who was in Shapley's office when Hubble's letter about the Cepheids arrived, Shapley held it out and said something like, 'Here is the letter that has destroyed my universe.'

Today we know Andromeda is even farther than Hubble thought: about 2.5 million light-years away. Hubble's number was too small because astronomers did not yet know that there are two different kinds of Cepheid stars with different brightnesses. But his main conclusion was completely right. When you look at Andromeda tonight, the light entering your eye left that galaxy about 2.5 million years ago, long before modern humans existed.

sections.heading: A Universe Full of Galaxies
paragraphs: It is hard to imagine how big a change this was. Before 1925, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was everything. After 1925, the Milky Way was just one galaxy, and the sky was sprinkled with others, each one an enormous city of stars. Every faint spiral smudge on every photographic plate was suddenly a whole galaxy. The universe had grown in size not by a little bit, but by an amount almost impossible to picture.

Andromeda itself turned out to be a giant. Modern measurements show its main disk is about 150,000 light-years across, somewhat bigger than our own Milky Way, and it contains perhaps a trillion stars. It is also coming toward us at roughly 300 kilometers per second. Astronomers have calculated that the two galaxies might collide and merge billions of years from now, though newer studies suggest this is far from certain.

Hubble went on to sort galaxies by shape. In 1926 he created the scheme now called the Hubble sequence, sometimes drawn as a tuning fork. On the handle are elliptical galaxies, smooth balls and ovals of stars. Then the fork splits into two prongs: ordinary spiral galaxies, with arms winding out from the center, and barred spirals, where the arms start from the ends of a straight bar of stars through the middle. Galaxies without any clear shape he called irregular. Astronomers still use his labels today.

sections.heading: Everything Is Rushing Apart
paragraphs: Remember Vesto Slipher from Part 12? Starting in 1912 at Lowell Observatory in Arizona, he had measured the speeds of spiral nebulae using the Doppler shift: light from something moving away from us is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, called a redshift. Slipher found that most spirals were racing away from us, some at hundreds of kilometers per second. Nobody knew why.

Now Hubble could measure distances. All he needed were more speeds, especially for very faint, very distant galaxies. That job fell largely to Milton Humason, the former mule driver. Getting a spectrum of a faint galaxy was brutally hard. The light was so feeble that Humason sometimes had to keep the telescope pointed perfectly at the same spot across more than one night, guiding by hand in the cold dark dome while the photographic plate slowly soaked up light. He became the best in the world at it.

In 1929 Hubble published a short paper with a simple graph. Along one side he put distance; along the other, speed. The dots were scattered, but they clearly made a rising line: the farther away a galaxy was, the faster it was moving away from us. In 1931 Hubble and Humason extended the result to galaxies much farther away, and the pattern held. This rule, speed equals a constant number times distance, became known as Hubble's law.

What does it mean? Imagine a loaf of raisin bread rising in the oven. As the dough swells, every raisin moves away from every other raisin. A raisin right next to you drifts away slowly, but a raisin on the far side of the loaf moves away much faster, because there is more dough between you to stretch. And it does not matter which raisin you sit on; from every raisin, all the others seem to be moving away. That is what the galaxies were doing. The universe itself is expanding.

But Hubble was not the first to put this idea together, and fair credit matters here. In 1927 a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist named Georges Lemaître had published a paper showing that Albert Einstein's theory of gravity allowed for an expanding universe, and that if the universe was expanding, galaxies' speeds should rise with their distance. Using Slipher's speeds and the best distances available, he even estimated the expansion rate. Sadly, his paper appeared in a Belgian journal that few astronomers elsewhere read. Lemaître recalled that when he told Einstein about his idea, Einstein said his math was correct but his physics was 'abominable.' Einstein later changed his mind after the observations came in, and in 1931 he visited Mount Wilson and met Hubble.

Lemaître went further. If everything is flying apart now, then long ago everything must have been packed together. In 1931 he proposed that the universe began from what he called a 'primeval atom.' This was the first version of what we now call the Big Bang theory.

So the discovery of the expanding universe belongs to several people: Slipher, who measured the speeds; Leavitt, whose ruler made distances possible; Lemaître, who predicted and first estimated the pattern; and Hubble and Humason, who nailed it down with the Hooker telescope. In 2018, members of the International Astronomical Union voted to recommend calling it the Hubble-Lemaître law, and about 78 percent of those who voted said yes.

sections.heading: The 200-Inch Giant of Palomar
paragraphs: Even the Hooker was not enough for George Ellery Hale. To see galaxies even farther away, he wanted a mirror twice as wide, 200 inches (5.1 meters), which would collect four times as much light. In 1928 he wrote a magazine article called 'The Possibilities of Large Telescopes', and that same year he won a grant of 6 million dollars from the Rockefeller Foundation, an enormous sum at the time. The new observatory would be run by the California Institute of Technology, Caltech, which Hale had helped grow into a top science university. A site was chosen on Palomar Mountain in northern San Diego County, far from the bright city lights that were starting to spoil the sky over Mount Wilson.

The first plan was to make the mirror out of fused quartz, a super-pure glass that hardly changes shape when it warms or cools. The General Electric company tried for years, but the quartz disks kept failing and the costs climbed. So the job went to Corning Glass Works in Corning, New York, which made a special heat-resistant glass called Pyrex, the same kind of glass used for baking dishes. Pyrex expands much less than ordinary glass when heated, so a Pyrex mirror would keep its shape better as the night air cooled.

Casting a 200-inch disk had never been done. To keep it from being impossibly heavy, the engineers designed a mold with a pattern of blocks underneath, so the back of the mirror would be a honeycomb of ribs instead of solid glass. That cut the amount of glass needed from over 40 tons to about 20. On 25 March 1934, in front of reporters and a crowd of visitors, workers ladled the glowing glass into the mold. But the heat made some of the blocks in the mold break loose and float up through the molten glass. That first disk was ruined. (It still exists and is displayed at the Corning Museum of Glass.)

Corning tried again. The second disk was cast on 2 December 1934. Glass this thick must cool extremely slowly, or it will crack from uneven shrinking. The disk was held at a high temperature for over a month, then cooled bit by bit for about ten months. Finally, the disk was ready.

On 26 March 1936 the 20-ton disk left Corning on a specially prepared railroad car, standing on its edge inside a protective steel crate. Sixteen days later, on 10 April 1936, it arrived at the Caltech optical shop in Pasadena.

Then came the grinding and polishing, which lasted about eleven and a half years, slowed down by World War II, when many workers left for war jobs. Over those years about 10,000 pounds (about 4.5 tonnes) of glass were ground away, leaving a mirror of about 14.5 tons with a curve accurate to a few millionths of a centimeter. Instead of silver, the finished mirror was coated with a thin layer of aluminum, which lasts longer.

George Ellery Hale never saw it finished. He died on 21 February 1938. On 3 June 1948, the great telescope was dedicated and given his name: the Hale Telescope. Its moving parts weigh about 530 tons, yet it is balanced so well that it can be turned precisely to follow the stars. On 26 January 1949, Edwin Hubble took the telescope's first official photograph, of a small fan-shaped nebula called NGC 2261.

The Hale Telescope was the largest effective telescope in the world for about 25 years. A Soviet telescope with a 6-meter mirror was finished in the mid-1970s but never worked as well, and only in 1993 did the 10-meter Keck telescope in Hawaii clearly beat it. The 200-inch is still used for research today. Hubble himself died in 1953, a few years after taking that first photograph. Every bigger telescope since has stood on the shoulders of the giant mirrors Hale dreamed up.

Those giant mirrors did not work by magic, though. Every one of them, from Galileo's little tube to the 200-inch, relies on the same few rules of light. Before we go further, let's open up a telescope and see exactly how it pulls off its tricks.

deepDive: Hubble's 1929 graph gave an expansion rate of about 500 kilometers per second per megaparsec (a megaparsec is about 3.26 million light-years). Today's value is about 70, roughly seven times smaller. Why was Hubble so far off? His distances were too short. In the early 1950s Walter Baade, using the Palomar 200-inch, showed that there are two different populations of Cepheid variable stars with different true brightnesses; astronomers had been calibrating Andromeda's Cepheids with the wrong kind. Correcting this roughly doubled the size of the known universe overnight. Other errors followed: some of Hubble's 'brightest stars' in distant galaxies were actually glowing gas clouds. Allan Sandage and others spent decades pushing the number down. The difference mattered enormously. If you run the expansion backward, the expansion rate gives a rough age of the universe. Hubble's 500 implied about 2 billion years, less than the age of the Earth as measured from radioactive rocks, which was a serious puzzle. Modern values give about 13.8 billion years. Today there is a new argument called the Hubble tension. Measurements using nearby stars and supernovae tend to give about 73, while calculations from the afterglow of the Big Bang give about 67 to 68. The gap is small but stubborn, and some astronomers think it may hint at new physics. There is also a historical puzzle. When Lemaître's 1927 paper was translated into English in 1931, the section estimating the expansion rate was left out. Some writers suspected someone was protecting Hubble's priority. In 2011 the astrophysicist Mario Livio found letters showing that Lemaître himself removed those paragraphs, apparently because newer data had made them out of date. Historians also stress that Hubble, in 1929, was cautious about saying the universe was expanding; he described an empirical relation between redshift and distance and left the interpretation open. The 2018 IAU recommendation to say 'Hubble-Lemaître law' was a vote by members, not a binding rule, but it reflects a growing effort to give credit fairly.
funFact: The very first 200-inch mirror disk that Corning cast in 1934 failed, and instead of being thrown away it was kept and is now displayed at the Corning Museum of Glass in New York.
